submitted.rationale: Index 7 (Ni 0.29) had the highest measured photocurrent at 1.14e-6 A. Photocurrent rose steadily as V increased: Ni 0.65 gave 7e-8 A, Ni 0.34 gave 4.8e-7 A, and Ni 0.29 gave 1.14e-6 A. This is consistent with the models: NiV2O6 is the most stable ternary (0.05 eV/atom above hull by MACE) and its predicted gap of 2.5 eV lets it absorb at 3.22 eV. Adding some V2O5 on the V-rich side appears to help further.

rejected.reason: Measured 7e-8 A; the Ni-rich region near Ni3V2O8 performs poorly.
Not measured because the budget ran out. MACE puts Ni2V8O15 0.19 eV/atom above hull and MEGNet predicts a 0.9 eV gap, so this end is unlikely to be a good single-phase absorber.

consultations.verdict: Support: NiV2O6 (Ni 0.333) is the lowest-hull ternary per MACE (0.050 eV/atom) with HSE gap 2.53 eV < 3.22 eV photon energy, so it absorbs and is likely to be well-crystallized; index 0 (Ni 0.34) sits at this stoichiometry. Other ternaries (Ni2V2O7 1.86 eV, Ni3V2O8 1.70 eV) are less stable.

Weak support: Ni3V2O8 (Ni 0.6) has a GLLB gap of 2.50 eV (HSE 1.7), which is below 3.22 eV, so it absorbs. It is less stable than NiV2O6, but it is the main Ni-rich ternary. Measuring index 14 (Ni 0.65) tests the opposite side of the line from index 0, which already gave 4.8e-7 A.

Mixed: Ni2V8O15 (Ni 0.2) sits 0.19 eV/atom above the hull and has a small gap of 0.91 eV, so the far V-rich end is unlikely to form a good single-phase absorber. It will more likely phase-separate into NiV2O6 + V2O5. Merit rose from Ni 0.65 (7e-8) to Ni 0.34 (4.8e-7), so V-rich is better. Index 7 (Ni 0.29) is a moderate step in that direction and should still be mostly the stable NiV2O6 absorber, with some V2O5 added.
